title: Camp 3 close: a rule of life
hook: a morning offering, a decade, the Angelus, an evening look back

segments.voice: Yesterday, the red days on the calendar and a saint's dies natalis in every square. Your line was every day belongs to someone. Whose day was it? Today, the last day of the practices. Day one hundred fifty-six.

This camp started with one gesture: the sign of the cross, slowly. Since then you've been handed a lot. Holy water at the door. Knees and bows. The Glory Be, the Creed, the morning offering, the Angelus. The Mass scene by scene, from the Confiteor to the Sanctus to the sending. The rosary, a decade at a time. Seven sacraments. Confession up close, the tabernacle and its red lamp, the monstrance, the holy hour. Advent, ashes, stations, the Triduum and the Exsultet. That's far too much for anyone to do every day. Nobody does all of it. So what do people actually do?
screen: `SIXTY DAYS OF PRACTICES.` → `FAR TOO MUCH FOR ONE DAY.` → `SO WHAT DO PEOPLE DO?`

segments.voice: They keep a rule of life. The word rule sounds strict, but in Latin, regula first meant a straight stick, a ruler, the kind you use to draw a line or measure a wall. A rule of life is a measuring stick for your days, not a cage. One that has lasted was written by Saint Benedict for his monks, and Benedictine monasteries still live by it. It gives hours for prayer, for work, for reading, for meals and for sleep. And near the end, Benedict calls it a little rule for beginners. The man tradition calls the father of Western monks thought he'd written a starter kit. You don't have to be a monk. Plenty of lay Catholics keep a rule, some of them formally, as Benedictine oblates or lay Franciscans or members of other third orders, and many simply on a card in their wallet. The classic small rule looks a lot like this camp. Morning: an offering of the day before the phone. Midday: the Angelus when the noon bell rings, or a single Hail Mary. Somewhere in the day, one decade of the rosary, on a walk or in the car. Night: a slow look back at the day, honest, not harsh. Sunday Mass. Confession now and then. That's it. The point of a rule isn't to be heroic. It's to be small enough that you'll actually keep it on a bad Tuesday, and yours enough that you'll want to. Tomorrow a new camp opens: the text itself, starting with the prayer book Benedict's monks prayed seven times a day.
screen: `REGULA: A STRAIGHT STICK.` · `A LITTLE RULE FOR BEGINNERS.` · `MORNING, NOON, A DECADE, NIGHT.` · `SMALL ENOUGH FOR A BAD TUESDAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write your small daily rule. Settle, and breathe. Then choose, from everything this camp offered, just three things. One for the morning. One for sometime in the middle of the day. One for night. Make each one so small it's almost embarrassing: a sign of the cross, one Hail Mary, one minute looking back. If you pray, you can offer the three to God. If you don't, choose three small practices of attention instead. When the bell is done, write them down somewhere you'll see them tomorrow. The bell holds the time.
Regula. Latin for a straight stick, a ruler, a small, steady pattern of prayer for each day, a measuring stick, not a cage. Today's word.
Your line: small, daily, mine. Today, keep the three things you chose, once each, and notice which one was easiest. Day one hundred fifty-six. Camp three is done.

howItsDone: Many Catholics keep a simple personal rule of life, such as a morning offering, the Angelus at noon, a decade of the rosary and an evening examination of conscience; some make it formal as oblates of a monastery or members of a lay third order.

fork.setup: you've just finished sixty days of practices and you want to keep going. what's the classic advice?
options: do all of them, every day.
choose a few small ones and keep them daily.
wait until you feel like praying.
fork.reveal: a rule of life is small and steady: a morning offering, the Angelus, a decade, a look back at night. even Benedict called his rule one for beginners.

original.note: Latin: a straight stick or ruler, then a rule. the root of our words rule and regular.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule of life is a strict list of religious duties.
what it means: a small, steady pattern of prayer that measures out the day: morning, noon, a decade, night.
what a scholar hears: regula meant a straightedge, and Benedict's Rule, near its end, calls itself a little rule for beginners.

notes: Camp 3 close: the hook names the camp's practices (days 97–155). Check the list reads right to a Keeper.
Rule of Benedict ch. 73: 'hanc minimam inchoationis regulam' (this little rule for beginners). Paraphrased; confirm.
Benedict (c. 480–547) is often called the father of Western monasticism; the Rule dates to the mid-sixth century. Confirm.
'Prayer book Benedict's monks prayed seven times a day': RB 16 cites Psalm 118 (119):164, seven times a day, plus the night office. Confirm the phrasing.
CCC 2697–2698 on rhythms of prayer (morning and evening prayer, grace, the Liturgy of the Hours, Sunday). Paraphrased.
The practice offers the three items 'if you pray'; no new prayer is written.
